@@135682233 <h> An energy transition driven by ethics <p> " Fossil fuel dependency is ripping away national security and sovereignty , and replacing it with subservience and rising costs , " UN climate change arm executive secretary Simon Stiell told European Union officials and Ministers in Brussels on March 16 , 2026 , against the backdrop of the U.S.-Israel-Iran war . He added that the disruption serves as an " abject lesson " on the pitfalls of banking on fossil fuels . <p> The war in West Asia has disproportionately affected economies such as India which gets nearly 60% of its crude oil from the region . The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has forced state-run refineries to declare force majeure -- an act of god . Pushing a country like India to abandon its remaining coal or domestic gas reserves without a take-off ramp could lead to industrial collapse . <p> The West used fossil fuels to build its strategic reserves and today ca n't deny India and other countries like it the same opportunities , especially as the latter waits for its renewables infrastructure to mature and expand @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fossil fuels from West Asia is obviously why its economy is currently hostage to the region 's geopolitical crisis . <h> Dependence on minerals <p> Mr. Stiell et al . have argued that renewables are immune to such blockades , which is true in part : if the flow of fossil fuels stops today -- it is pinched in the Strait of Hormuz -- the ' flow ' of energy also stops , because we burn fossil fuels to release energy . With renewables , the critical minerals are not the source of energy itself . Once the state has set up solar panels and erected wind turbines , their ability to generate energy can not be embargoed because they will operate as long as the sun shines and the wind blows . <p> However , critical minerals still represent a significant bottleneck , with additional complications such as the number of industries that need them -- from consumer electronics to missile targeting , with the renewable energy sector somewhere in between . The supply chains for many minerals are even more concentrated than oil . The Organization of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ global oil production . And while the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Australia plus Chile extract most of the cobalt and lithium , respectively , a single country -- China -- currently processes almost 60% of the world 's lithium , 70% of its cobalt , and 90% of rare-earth elements . <p> With renewable energy also making intensive use of hardware , a blockade of the required components , whether it be turbine blades or magnets based on rare earth minerals , would be just as effective as one of oil . At that point , it is once again a question of whether war could break out between the world 's primary mineral-processing hubs . <h> Fossil versus mineral <p> The " abject lesson " is only so abject because of the prevailing oil situation . If , say , the West Asia conflict had not begun and Brent crude was $65 a barrel , the trade-off for renewables could return to seeming like a moral luxury -- in turn retrenching the value of ' shock ' events like wars to push the world away from fossil @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ et al . are smart to seize the chance . <p> Without a war driving prices up , the high upfront capital expenditure for renewables is less attractive to governments . If oil is cheap , the payback period for a large offshore wind farm might be 15 years ; if gas prices jump 50% , this period could shrink to 4-5 years . In other words , sans a war , governments would have continued to place fiscal responsibility before energy sovereignty . <p> In the same scenario , the world 's dependencies on the critical mineral supply chain presents itself as a scarier prospect . If West Asia is stable and oil is flowing , the U.S. and its allies would likely view the option of trading West Asian oil for Chinese minerals as a net loss in strategic autonomy , which could encourage countries to reshore mineral mining and processing capabilities even before the energy transition picks up pace . <p> For India , a more stable supply of oil together with its arguably excessive focus on easing business could render its off-ramp into a long and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and cheap imported gas to power industrial growth while waiting for renewables to mature . <p> In other words , the Strait of Hormuz blockade could be forcing India to accelerate investments in renewables simply because it has no choice . <h> Fear not an effective tool <p> Mr. Stiell is in effect wielding fear as his primary tool , especially when he says " dependency is ripping away national security " . The effects of fear never last -- especially when countries imagine new ways to outmanoeuvre these threats . What ultimately matters is ethics . The virtue of renewables should be debated , and adopted , in order to save the planet rather than for saving the economy for another month . <p> This also matters because when oil is cheap , the environmental damage of mining lithium , or human rights issues in Congolese cobalt mines are scrutinised more heavily by the public -- and while this is as it should be , it should not just be because oil is cheap . <h> Comments <p> Comments have to be in English , and in full sentences @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ abide by our community guidelines for posting your comments . <p> We have migrated to a new commenting platform . To be considered a heat wave , the temperatures have to be outside the historical averages for a given area . <p> They form when high pressure systems trap warm air in a particular area . This forces air to sink and compress , creating a dome of heat , which increases temperatures at the surface @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more often ? <p> Scientists have long understood that human-induced climate change would cause the Earth to heat up . <p> " We always knew that climate change was going to bring more extreme heat days , and that was going to start earlier in the year , " says Dr. David Eisenman , professor of medicine at UCLA whose research focuses on the public health impacts of extreme heat . " And I think we 're seeing that now . " <p> The trend has become especially apparent over the last few years . Global temperatures from the past three years averaged more than 1.5 ? C above the pre-industrial level , and the last decade has been the warmest on record . ( One or two years of global temperatures above 1.5 ? C does not mean the world has passed the Paris Agreement goal to limit warming to 1.5 ? C. Scientists determine long-term temperature changes on timescales of decades . ) <p> Advertisement <p> While it might not seem like much , even incremental increases in global temperatures have a big impact on our climate . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ temperature by one and a half or two degrees , that really does n't tell us everything , " says Eisenman . " What really happens is that it shifts a curve of the probability of extreme heat days . So instead of seeing , say , 90 degree days only 5% of the time , it now starts to happen 10 or 15% of the time . These extreme heat days are just the natural result of shifting the average temperature by even a small number of degrees . @@135748829 <p> Once-full rivers become seasonal , aquifers turn saline ; as groundwater levels sink , the ground itself may begin to subside . Pretty soon , one is staring at the bottom of the barrel . <p> " This is not a water crisis anymore . This is water bankruptcy , " Madani says . <p> Once things reach this point , the familiar remedies of water cuts and water trains make little difference . It will take new approaches to craft a way forward . <p> The first step is acknowledging the irreversible nature of the damage . When applied to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that stakeholders , whether farmers , city-dwellers or the government , will each seek to meet their interests , and may choose competitive rather than cooperative strategies , based on what they think others will likely do . <p> Game theory has been applied to the study and modelling of human systems since about the 1940s . Madani has been successful in integrating game theory into water management models . His research explores the mismatch between optimal plans and real motivations at the consumer level , across a wide range of issues , from groundwater depletion and irrigation conflicts to climate-driven scarcity . <p> In a simplified example , if a farmer sees his neighbour pump out groundwater amid a shortage , he will do the same , even if that leads to a shared collapse . <p> Factor such fears , competition and suspicion into models , and sustainable water management begins to look rather different . <p> New approaches could involve restructuring water rights , pricing and restrictions , no matter how unpopular the move ; thus reducing demand through policy . But in the next 30 years , the people who will bear the brunt of that catastrophe -- who will be dispossessed , uprooted , and exposed to the worst of the elements -- will be those who are already on the other side of society 's walls . <p> In the 1930s , rolling black dust storms blanketed America 's Great Plains , uprooting topsoil and crops across 100 million acres of land . The clouds billowed as far east as New York , choking farm economies in the middle of the country and sending millions of people on the move . The black blizzards seemed to many like divine judgment ; actually , they had their origins at least partly in human action . Years of deep plowing and overgrazing had eroded the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ now as the Dust Bowl . <p> As these storms darkened the prairies , farmers and laborers alike sought refuge . Many of them traveled hundreds of miles to California and other havens . Despite the passage of New Deal programs to aid these " Okies , " many did not receive a warm welcome in their new homes , because some saw them as interlopers competing for housing and jobs . In one ugly episode , Los Angeles Police Department Chief James Edgar Davis stationed more than 100 officers along the California border to enforce a " bum blockade " against migrants . California had made it a misdemeanor for any citizen to transport an " indigent " person into the state , a law that was later overturned by the Supreme Court . The Court 's decision became part of the established basis for a right that many Americans take for granted -- the ability to travel freely across state lines . <p> As Octavia Butler believed , America 's past is a good place to start when trying to predict how climate change will reconfigure its society @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , sudden movements of people driven by disaster and local changes in climate . These upheavals have always caused tensions , and those tensions have shaped the American social order in many ways . <p> Within the U.S. today , people are again moving because of disasters , and because of the slow-grind attrition of heat , flooding , and rising insurance rates . Earlier this year , the nonprofit Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre found that disasters had caused 11 million evacuations or relocations in the previous 12 months . These numbers will climb . Without interstate coordination and federal relief funding , workers and politicians in receiving zones may try to keep out newcomers -- especially poor ones , arriving en masse on the heels of a particular disaster -- as they did during the Dust Bowl . <p> In his forthcoming book , aptly titled North : The Future of Post-Climate America , Keenan anticipates a major climate migration -- out of the South to cooler , less volatile climes -- driven partly by disaster but also by a simple preference for milder weather . Over the past @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has been the steady relocation of people -- and of the country 's center of gravity -- to the Sun Belt . Southern metropolises such as Atlanta , Houston , Dallas , Phoenix , and Charlotte expanded rapidly . But , according to Keenan , climate change has essentially stopped growth in southward movement , and northern cities are seeing fewer outflows and greater influxes of people . <p> Keenan 's observation aligns with a recent study published by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco , which found that for decades , hotter places tended to grow faster than colder ones . But from 2010 to 2020 , that pattern ceased . The places facing existential climate risks -- especially those in the Deep South -- are mostly in states that have long been considered politically uncompetitive , where neither party expends much effort or money to gain votes . Where risk and disinvestment come together in America , democracy has always suffered . In many ways , crisis is revelatory , and we know that disasters expose cracks in society . If there is a sliver of a chance of averting the scenarios I 've laid out , it will have to come by the hands of a movement that finally repairs those cracks . <p> It is easiest , as I have done , to imagine those faults persisting and widening , in which case the worst conclusions about our future physical and political climates are likely to hold true . @@135832027 <p> Biofuels are often promoted as a cleaner alternative to fossil fuels , but their environmental and social impacts are far from straightforward . Just Have a Think examines the complexities of biofuel production , including the significant challenges posed by land use changes and carbon emissions . For instance , the cultivation of first-generation biofuels like palm oil has been linked to deforestation and habitat destruction , undermining their supposed sustainability . These unintended consequences highlight the need to critically assess whether biofuels can genuinely contribute to a low-carbon future or if they risk perpetuating existing environmental issues . <p> In this explainer , you 'll gain insight into the different types of biofuels , from first-generation crops to advanced options like Sustainable Aviation Fuels ( SAFs ) . Explore how land use demands and indirect emissions affect their overall carbon footprint and understand why scalability remains a major hurdle for second-generation biofuels . Additionally , this overview provide more insights into the socioeconomic impacts of biofuel production , particularly in vulnerable regions and considers whether alternative energy solutions like solar and wind might offer more sustainable pathways forward @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Key Takeaways : <p> Biofuels are categorized into first-generation ( food crops ) , second-generation ( non-food sources ) , and Sustainable Aviation Fuels ( SAFs ) , each with distinct benefits and challenges , including environmental and scalability concerns . <p> Large-scale biofuel production raises significant land use issues , such as deforestation , habitat destruction and biodiversity loss , making renewable energy sources like solar and wind more efficient alternatives . <p> The " carbon-neutral " label for biofuels is misleading , as their production often generates substantial greenhouse gas emissions , sometimes rivaling or exceeding those of fossil fuels . <p> Biofuel production has socioeconomic impacts , including displacement of communities , disruption of livelihoods and perpetuation of fossil fuel infrastructure , raising concerns about equity and justice . <p> Biofuels are fuels derived from organic materials , often referred to as biomass . They are categorized into three primary types , each with distinct production methods and environmental implications : <p> First-generation biofuels : These are produced from food crops such as corn , sugarcane and palm oil . While they are widely used , their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ higher food prices and contributing to environmental degradation . Issues such as deforestation , soil depletion and water resource strain are common concerns associated with these biofuels . <p> Second-generation biofuels : Also known as advanced biofuels , these are derived from non-food sources like agricultural residues , wood and other cellulosic materials . They aim to address the shortcomings of first-generation biofuels by reducing competition with food crops and minimizing environmental harm . However , challenges such as high production costs and scalability hinder their widespread adoption . <p> Sustainable Aviation Fuels ( SAFs ) : A specialized category of biofuels designed for aviation , SAFs are promoted as a way to decarbonize air travel . Despite their potential , SAF production faces significant hurdles , including limited availability of raw materials and questions about their long-term sustainability and environmental impact . <p> While each type of biofuel offers potential benefits , their overall contribution to a sustainable energy future remains uncertain , particularly when compared to other renewable energy sources . <h> Land Use : A Growing Concern <p> The large-scale production of biofuels requires vast amounts of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( ILUC ) . For example , forests may be cleared to make way for biofuel crops , resulting in deforestation , habitat destruction and a loss of biodiversity . This displacement of natural ecosystems not only harms wildlife but also releases substantial amounts of stored carbon into the atmosphere , effectively negating the environmental benefits of biofuels . <p> In comparison , renewable energy sources such as solar and wind power are far more efficient in terms of land use . A solar farm , for instance , can generate significantly more energy per acre than biofuel crops , making it a more practical and sustainable solution for reducing greenhouse gas emissions without compromising valuable land resources . The land-intensive nature of biofuels raises critical questions about their feasibility as a long-term energy solution . <h> Are Biofuels Truly Carbon Neutral ? <p> Biofuels are often marketed as " carbon-neutral " because the plants used to produce them absorb carbon dioxide during their growth . However , this label can be misleading . The cultivation , processing and transportation of biofuel crops generate substantial greenhouse gas emissions . For @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ directly linked to deforestation in tropical regions , releasing vast amounts of stored carbon and exacerbating climate change . <p> Indirect land use changes further complicate the carbon footprint of biofuels . When agricultural land is repurposed for biofuel crops , food production is often displaced to previously uncultivated areas , leading to additional deforestation and emissions . In some cases , the total emissions associated with biofuels can rival or even exceed those of the fossil fuels they are intended to replace . This raises serious doubts about the environmental benefits of biofuels and their role in reducing global carbon emissions . <h> Socioeconomic and Political Impacts <p> The production of biofuels has far-reaching social and economic consequences , particularly in developing regions . These impacts disproportionately affect marginalized populations , raising critical questions about equity and global justice . <p> Moreover , the integration of biofuels into existing energy systems can perpetuate reliance on fossil fuel infrastructure . This approach risks diverting attention and resources away from renewable energy technologies that offer more fantastic potential . <h> Biofuels in Aviation : A Limited Solution <p> The aviation industry has embraced Sustainable Aviation Fuels ( SAFs ) as a means to reduce its carbon footprint . While SAFs can lower the carbon intensity of air travel , their production faces significant constraints , including limited supplies of waste materials and the same land use concerns that affect other biofuels . Additionally , SAFs do not address the fundamental inefficiencies of aviation , which remains one of the most carbon-intensive modes of transportation . <p> Emerging alternatives , such as electric planes and high-speed rail systems , offer more sustainable options for reducing the environmental impact of short-haul travel . Although these technologies are still in development , they hold significant promise for transforming the transportation sector and reducing its reliance on carbon-intensive fuels . <h> Balancing Benefits and Limitations <p> Advanced biofuels and waste-based fuels show potential as lower-carbon alternatives , particularly when derived from non-food sources like @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ scalability and environmental impacts must be carefully managed to avoid repeating the mistakes associated with first-generation biofuels . Policymakers must strike a delicate balance between fostering economic stability and addressing the urgent need to combat climate change . This includes exploring alternative energy solutions that offer greater long-term benefits without compromising social or environmental integrity . <h> Are Biofuels a Step Forward or a Step Back ? <p> The critical question remains : Are biofuels genuinely advancing the transition away from fossil fuels , or are they merely allowing the fossil fuel industry to adapt and persist ? Renewable energy sources like solar and wind , combined with advancements in transportation technologies , provide more effective and sustainable pathways @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ evaluated , it is crucial to consider not only their immediate benefits but also their long-term impacts on the environment , society and the global energy transition . Biofuels may play a role in the energy mix , but they are not the comprehensive solution they are often portrayed to be . Instead , a broader focus on truly renewable energy sources and innovative technologies will be essential for achieving a sustainable and equitable energy future .

" <p> " I definitely think they look cute , " she says . <p> Cute -- but also cutthroat . This fish is an ambush predator .
